Chapter 4: Navigating Cultural Identity and Belonging
Imagine living in a world where cultures blend together, and the lines between them start to fade. Finding out who you are can sometimes feel like walking a tightrope, can't it?
Through the father’s letters to Su Yen, we get a window into what it really means to belong—not just to a family or a community, but to a heritage that can be both a source of pride and, at times, a real challenge.
He looks back on his own childhood, growing up in a home where several languages danced around the dinner table, and traditions from different backgrounds mixed and mingled. There were moments when he felt stuck between worlds—feeling too traditional for some, too modern for others. At school, he sometimes wondered which parts of himself he should share, and which ones he should keep hidden.
Now, as Su Yen grows up in a multicultural society, these questions feel even more pressing. Her father wants her to see her diverse background not as something heavy to carry, but as a real strength. He shares a story about a friend who always tried to fit in—changing her accent, her mannerisms, just to match those around her. But over time, she realized that real belonging doesn’t come from blending in. It comes from owning what makes you unique.
The father also talks about how tough it can be to pass down cultural values in a world that’s always changing. He remembers family gatherings, where elders shared stories about their homeland, hoping to keep that sense of pride and continuity alive. But there were also moments of tension—when younger relatives questioned old customs, or pushed for something new. It became so clear to him that culture isn’t frozen in time; it grows and shifts with each generation, shaped by new experiences and new perspectives.
He encourages Su Yen to stay curious about her roots—to ask questions, to dig into the stories that make up her family’s past. At the same time, he wants her to create her own path, blending the best of different worlds in a way that feels true to who she is. He knows it won’t always be easy. There’ll be times when she feels like an outsider, or wonders where she really belongs.
But to him, identity isn’t something you simply inherit. It’s something you build, piece by piece, through your choices, your relationships, and your experiences. He hopes Su Yen will take pride in her heritage, but also find the courage to let go of what doesn’t fit anymore. In a world that often pressures us to blend in, he wants her to remember: it’s more than okay to be different, to stand out, and to define yourself in your own way.
For the father, these reflections go deeper than just cultural pride—they’re about empathy and understanding. He reminds Su Yen that we all carry our own stories, our own struggles with fitting in. And by staying open and compassionate, she’ll be able to build bridges across differences, finding common ground with the people around her.
